For a business card, shop window, or packaging insert, use the profile link. It keeps working as you post, and the follow button sits one tap from the landing screen.
Use a video link when the code has exactly one job: a launch poster, or a sticker on the product that points at the ad. The link pins one video ID. Delete that video and the code goes dead.
Hashtag links work, but they show everyone's posts on the tag, not just yours. Good for a campaign landing page, wrong for a business card.
What happens when someone scans it
link opens, prompt to switch to the app

The handoff is a prompt, not a guarantee. Some phones show a full-screen "Open in TikTok?" banner, others show a slim bar at the top, and a few open the mobile site with no prompt at all. People tap through most of the time, but some don't, and you should assume a slice of scans land on the web version.

Two consequences worth planning for. A scan is not a follow: the person still has to tap Follow after landing, so the code gets them to the door, not through it. And the mobile web version loads slower than the app, which matters if the code is on packaging where attention is already thin.
A private account shows scanners the profile shell and a request button. No QR code can get around that setting.
TikTok's own QR code, and when to use it instead
The app has a QR code built in: open your profile, tap the share icon, choose QR code. Free, and it works — inside TikTok.

The catch is who can read it. That code is meant for TikTok's own scanner. Scan it with an iPhone Camera app or a stock Android camera and you often get nothing at all, or a nudge to install TikTok first. On a phone screen, where the person already has the app open, that's fine. On a printed sticker, a shop window, or a menu, the scanner is a stranger holding a default camera app.

The code you make here is a standard QR code. Any camera reads it, and the link inside behaves the same as a typed URL. That's the entire difference, and it's the reason a printed code is worth generating separately from the in-app one.
One thing to watch: your handle is part of the URL. Rename the account and both codes break. Generate a fresh one after a rename, and replace anything already printed.

Keep the quiet zone. The blank margin around the pattern is how cameras find the code in the first place, and cropping it to fit a design is the single most common reason a printed code fails.
Test the proof with a phone before the print run. A code that reads on screen can fail on a curved bottle or a glossy label, and you find out after the boxes arrive.
